title: The coin that hasn't landed
subtitle: Your first qubit: superposition, measurement and the most honest randomness in the universe.

steps.title: Bits are coins on the floor
body: Every computer you've ever used stores information in bits: 0 or 1, heads or tails. The coin is always on the floor, one side up — even when nobody is looking.
A qubit is different. Before it's measured, it can be in a superposition: a combination of 0 and 1, each with a weight. Think of a coin still spinning in the air.
When you measure, the coin “lands”: you get 0 or 1. Which one? Physics doesn't decide that in advance — it only gives the odds.
steps.aside: The coin analogy is a starting point. In the next levels you'll see where it breaks — and that's where it gets good.

steps.title: Toss the quantum coin
steps.body: This circuit starts with a qubit in |0⟩ and applies the H gate (Hadamard), which sets it spinning. Measure a few times and see what happens.
steps.after: Half 0, half 1 — but no pattern at all in the sequence. Each measurement prepared a brand-new qubit and measured it. There's no “memory” and no trick: it's the purest chance nature has to offer.

steps.question: You measured a qubit in superposition and got 1. If you measure the same qubit again, without touching anything, what do you get?

options.why: Yes! Measuring “drops the coin”: afterwards, the qubit is exactly the result you saw. Measuring again confirms the 1.
That would be true if the coin started spinning again on its own. But measurement changes the state: after seeing 1, the qubit is in |1⟩.
The universe doesn't balance its books! There's no memory to “even out” — and the qubit is now in |1⟩.

steps.title: Build your own coin
steps.goal: Give the qubit a 50% chance of reading 0 and a 50% chance of reading 1.
hints: Click a gate in the palette, then an empty spot on the wire.
The gate that sets the qubit “spinning” starts with H.
steps.success: Coin in the air! Look at the bars: both results have the same height. And the arrow on the sphere lay down on the equator — that's where half-and-half superpositions live.

steps.title: Loaded coin
steps.goal: Now make the qubit read 1 with 100% certainty.
hints: No superposition needed here: you just want to flip the coin.
The X gate is the quantum “NOT”: it swaps 0 and 1.
steps.success: The X gate is the NOT of ordinary computers. The arrow went from the north pole (|0⟩) to the south pole (|1⟩).

steps.title: True randomness
steps.text: The “random” in your computer is almost always a well-disguised calculation: whoever knows the seed can predict everything. Quantum random number generators measure quantum phenomena — like vacuum fluctuations or photons hitting a half-silvered mirror — and produce sequences nobody can predict, not even in principle.
steps.source: E.g. the public quantum random number generator at the Australian National University (ANU).

options.text: The qubit is already 0 or 1; we just don't know which.
options.why: That's the “local hidden variable” idea, and experiments (Nobel Prize 2022) show nature doesn't work that way. Superposition is stranger than simple ignorance.

options.text: The qubit is 0 and 1 at the same time, and measurement picks one.
options.why: A popular phrase, but misleading: if it were just “both at once”, there would be no way to explain interference, which you'll see in the level on phase and interference.

options.text: A state with weights (amplitudes) for 0 and 1, which set the odds when you measure.
options.why: Exactly. Superposition is described by amplitudes — numbers that can even cancel out. They decide the measurement probabilities.

takeaways: A bit is 0 or 1. A qubit can be in superposition until it's measured.
Measuring gives a random result, with odds set by the state — and it changes the state.
The H gate creates a half-and-half superposition; the X gate swaps 0 and 1.
